title: Tods' Amendment
body: The Legal Member's new Sub-Montane Tracts Ryotwari Enactment is a marvel of drafting and, you are assured, a boon to the cultivator. At the Club dinner it is little Tods — six years old, ungovernable, fluent in the bazaar tongue his ayah taught him — who announces between mouthfuls what the bazaar says the new law will really do. ‘The ryots say it gives the land to the bunnias,’ says Tods, and asks for more pudding.

choices.label: Take the child's report seriously and propose an amendment.
choices.outcome: You draft a note embodying, in the language of the Secretariat, what a six-year-old had from a groom. The clause is amended. Somewhere a Legal Member pencils ‘Tods' Amendment’ in a margin, and never learns he was corrected by a child and a bazaar nobody thought to ask.

choices.label: Smile at the mite and pass the Enactment as drafted.
choices.outcome: You are not about to redraft an Act of the Government of India on the word of an infant, however fluent. The law goes through as written. In six months the cultivators have discovered what Tods knew at dinner, and the discovery reaches your desk as forty petitions in one week.

choices.label: Quietly send a man to the bazaar to check the child's tale.
choices.outcome: You have the thing looked into, discreetly, and it is every word true. You mend what you can without confessing where the intelligence came from. It is humbling to govern a district worse than a six-year-old understands it, and wiser not to say so aloud.

title: The Enlightenment of Pagett, M.P.
body: Mr. Pagett, a Radical Member newly off the boat, has come to study Indian Conditions for a fortnight. ‘The Congress,’ he tells you warmly, before his boxes are unstrapped, ‘speaks for the teeming millions. The whole country groans for self-government.’ He is your guest, your responsibility, and certain of everything. The cold weather is turning, and the hot weather, with the real education, is on its way.

choices.label: Show him the real, fractured district — caste, creed, and the cultivator who has never heard of Congress.
choices.outcome: You walk him through a country that refuses to fit his pamphlet: the tenant who fears his headman more than any Viceroy, two faiths that will not share a well, the peasant to whom Simla and London are the same distant rumour. Pagett's certainties wilt in the dust. He goes home wiser, and writes, alas, the same articles.

choices.label: Flatter his views, feed him well, and pack him off content.
choices.outcome: You give him the tour he came to have, agree with everything, and put him on the train still glowing. He will report that the local officials are sound fellows who quite understand the national aspiration. It costs you three dinners and teaches him nothing.

choices.label: Let a day of touring in the heat do the arguing.
choices.outcome: You say little and let the sun, the flies, and the twelve-hour march do the arguing. By evening the Member has stopped lecturing and begun asking questions. To the last of them — ‘How many of you govern all this?’ — you give him the figure, and he is quiet for the rest of the ride.

title: The Head of the District
body: The Secretariat, in a spasm of principle, has appointed Mr. Banerjee — able, honourable, Calcutta-educated, and Bengali — to hold charge of the Karara tract, a country of proud and turbulent men who have announced, with perfect courtesy and total conviction, that they will take no orders from a clerk of the plains. The appointment is just, and it may be the spark to a rising, and both facts lie in the same docket on your desk.

choices.label: Install him and back him with every man you have.
choices.outcome: You put Banerjee in his chair and stand behind it with the police. He is competent and unbowed; the tract seethes, tests him, and subsides, because the force behind him never blinks. Principle is upheld at the point of a bayonet, and the bayonets stay fixed the whole cold weather.

choices.label: Quietly arrange a safer posting for him elsewhere.
choices.outcome: You spare Banerjee the Karara and the Karara its rising, and concede in doing so that a good man may not rule where his face is wrong. ‘I quite understand,’ he says, and thanks you with a dignity that scalds. He goes on to serve, very well, somewhere easier.

choices.label: Tell Simla plainly the appointment courts a rising.
choices.outcome: You put your objection on paper, over your signature, and let the Secretariat own its choice. The appointment is quietly reconsidered; you are quietly entered as an officer who tells his betters what they do not care to hear. The entry outlasts the thanks.

title: The Men Who Would Be Kings
body: Two enormous, ragged Englishmen — loafers, deserters, it is never quite clear — present themselves at your camp with a Masonic handshake and a plan to walk beyond the frontier and make themselves kings of a country no map has properly seen. ‘We have signed a contrack,’ says the larger, producing a greasy paper. ‘No liquor and no women till the thing is done.’ They ask only that the sahib not wire ahead to have them stopped.

choices.label: Give them a drink, a warning, and let them go.
choices.outcome: You tell them the frontier eats such men, and they agree cheerfully and go anyway, as such men do. You never learn how it ended — only that one of them is said to have come crawling back, years later, with a tale no sane man believed and a thing wrapped in cloth that he would not show.

choices.label: Have them run out of the district at once.
choices.outcome: You are not in the business of speeding lunatics toward an international incident, and you have them escorted firmly to the railhead. Correct, dull, and a small theft from the world's stock of glorious catastrophe. They curse you from the carriage window, in style, the whole length of the platform.

choices.label: Slip them a letter of introduction and a nod.
choices.outcome: Against every regulation and most of your sense, you help them on their way, because a district is a dusty place and their madness is at least a large one. If it ever comes out that the magistrate franked two filibusters over the border it will not be your prestige that survives — but you will have your secret grin.

title: Thrown Away
body: Young Cottar — nineteen, raised soft and sheltered and sent out to a country that shelters no one — took a public rebuke over a trifle harder than the trifle deserved, rode out alone into the hot weather, and did not ride back. The Civil Surgeon has found him, and the revolver, and stands now in your office, not quite meeting your eye. ‘Cholera,’ he says. ‘For the sake of a mother in England who need never know.’

choices.label: Sign the merciful lie. Cholera it is.
choices.outcome: You put your name to a death certificate you know to be false, and a mother keeps a son who died bravely of fever instead of alone of despair. It is a kindness and a forgery, and the two will not separate. The station buries the Boy and its knowledge of him in the same hour, calls the whole thing very sad, and goes in to dinner.

choices.label: Record the truth, coldly and completely.
choices.outcome: You will not begin your rule with a lie, however kind, and you write the thing as it was. The paper is impeccable; the mother's letter, when it comes, cannot be answered by any paper; and the station sets you down as a man without the ordinary mercy. The letter stays in your desk for three years.

choices.label: Blame the system that broke him, and say so in the report.
choices.outcome: You write that the Boy was thrown away — sent out too young, worked too hard, rebuked too publicly, in a place that forgives none of it — and you name the machine that did it. It is true, it is unwelcome, and it will be quietly held against you by every man who suspects the same could be written of him.

title: Strickland of the Police
body: Strickland — the police officer the station thinks unsound because he vanishes for weeks and comes back knowing things — lays before you what a month living as a groom in the city's back lanes has taught him: who is arming, who is owed money by whom, which respectable men are not respectable. It is intelligence no honest method could have got; it would let you break trouble before it starts, and ruin a dozen men on a word. ‘Use it or burn it,’ he says. ‘I am going back either way.’

choices.label: Act on it — arrests, warnings, a quiet pre-emption.
choices.outcome: You use what Strickland got by deceit, and the trouble that was brewing never brews. The district is safer and does not know why, and a dozen men are watched or worse on the strength of a policeman who pretended to be their servant. It works. Most of the ugly things do.

choices.label: Thank him and decline to use it so got.
choices.outcome: You tell Strickland his methods are more than you can put your name to, and let the intelligence lie. He looks at you with the weary patience of a man who has seen squeamishness cost lives, salutes, and goes back to the lanes to learn things you will again decline to hear.

choices.label: Take the knowledge but keep it in reserve.
choices.outcome: You file what he brings against a rainy day, using none of it yet, letting it sit in your head like a loaded thing in a drawer. A man cannot keep clean hands and a full magazine together, and you have contrived, for the present, to hold neither.

title: Mrs Hauksbee Takes an Interest
body: Up at Simla, where the careers of the plains are made and unmade over tea, the celebrated Mrs Hauksbee — cleverer than the Secretariat and far better informed — has been heard to mention your name, not unkindly. A word from her in the right verandah can lift a man over the heads of his seniors; her disfavour has ended better men than you before they knew they were in it.

choices.label: Cultivate her — call, charm, be useful.
choices.outcome: You pay court to the drawing-room as assiduously as to the cutcherry, and it answers: your name begins to travel in the currents that matter, borne by a woman who moves the machinery of Empire without being allowed near its levers. It is the most useful and least dignified campaign of your year.

choices.label: Keep a cautious distance from Simla's intrigues.
choices.outcome: You decline to make your career in a hill-station drawing-room, and Mrs Hauksbee, who mistakes no one, marks you as a dull dog who will go just as far as his files carry him and no further. She is very often right about such things.

choices.label: Amuse her with honest gossip from the plains.
choices.outcome: You send her, now and then, a funny and indiscreet account of district life, asking nothing. She adores it, repeats it beautifully, and does you small unseen kindnesses for the pleasure of the correspondence. ‘My magistrate,’ she is heard to say, ‘is the only man in India who has never asked me for anything.’

title: The Matter of Jack Barrett
body: A powerful man — a name that signs your confidential reports — lets it be known, through the usual soft channels, that it would gratify him to see young Jack Barrett transferred to Fever Hill, the pestilential little station up the line from which men are carried out more often than posted away. Barrett is inconvenient to him. Barrett has a wife. The request is deniable, ordinary, and perfectly understood.

choices.label: Refuse, and make a dangerous enemy.
choices.outcome: You find Barrett unfit for Fever Hill and say so, and the soft channels go cold, and a name that matters adds yours to a private ledger of officers who did not oblige. You have kept a man alive and made your own advancement a good deal steeper. You would, you tell yourself, do it again.

choices.label: Sign the transfer. It is only a posting.
choices.outcome: You post Jack Barrett to Fever Hill with a stroke of the pen, and in eleven weeks the fever does what the powerful man could not decently do himself. You are thanked, obliquely, and advanced. The phrase on the order was ‘the needs of the service.’ You do not use that phrase again.

choices.label: Quietly warn Barrett to apply for leave.
choices.outcome: You cannot stop the posting, but you can see that Barrett hears, from nowhere in particular, that his health would be much better in the hills this season. He takes the hint and the leave and lives, puzzled; the powerful man is balked without ever seeing the hand; and you have done a decent thing in the only coin the system leaves you — the whisper.

title: The Bridge-Builders
body: Findlayson's great railway bridge over the river — three years' work, the pride of the Public Works, all but finished — stands in the path of the highest flood in living memory. ‘Every man and every boat the district can raise,’ begs the Chief Engineer, grey with sleeplessness. The same men and boats are the only thing that can lift the low villages out of the water. There is not enough of either for both.

choices.label: Throw the district's labour and boats at the bridge.
choices.outcome: You back the works, and Findlayson's bridge stands through the night by main force and a hair's breadth — a monument to what the Raj can do when it decides a thing shall not fall. The low villages, given what was left, fare worse. The bridge will carry trains for a hundred years. The villages will remember which the sahib chose to save.

choices.label: Send everything to lift the villages and let the river judge the bridge.
choices.outcome: You put the people before the pride of the Public Works, and the boats go to the rooftops instead of the piers. Fewer drown. In the grey morning the river has taken a span of Findlayson's bridge and three years of his life with it, and the Department will want to know, in writing, whose orders left it undefended.

choices.label: Split the effort and pray the river is merciful.
choices.outcome: You halve the district between the bridge and the villages, and thereby ask the flood to be reasonable. Floods are not. The bridge is damaged but stands; some villages are reached in time and some are not; and there is a stretch of that night, between the third boat and the fourth, that you never speak of afterwards.

title: The Mark of the Beast
body: On a night of drunken celebration, Fleete — a newcomer who holds his liquor worse than his tongue — grinds his cigar-butt into the forehead of the god Hanuman in the little temple by the bazaar. By morning the bazaar is silent in the way that precedes trouble, a leper has been seen at Fleete's gate, and the Civil Surgeon is using the word ‘fever’ for something he cannot name.

choices.label: Get Fleete out of the district quietly and say nothing.
choices.outcome: You have him carried off on the night train, cured by means no report will ever mention, and you spend the small hours learning things about your own certainties that you will spend years unlearning. The temple is quiet by morning. You are not.

choices.label: Post police at the temple and let the law be seen to stand.
choices.outcome: You answer an old darkness with constables and a firm hand, the Service issuing no other equipment for it. The trouble does not come, this time. Whether the constables prevented it, or something older chose to let it lie, is not a question the office forms provide for.

choices.label: Make a formal apology and reparation to the temple.
choices.outcome: You go, hat in hand and against every instinct of your rank, and make amends for the sahib's insult. The bazaar exhales; the priests are grave and satisfied; and the Club decides, over its brandy, that the young magistrate has knelt to superstition and will bear watching.

title: Without Benefit of Clergy
body: Holden of the Canals is dead of the fever, and in settling his affairs you find what the station never knew he had: a small shuttered house in the city, and in it a grave the size of a cradle, and a young woman with a grief that has no official standing whatever. She has no claim the law will hear, and nowhere the station will let her be. Holden's secret is now yours.

choices.label: See her quietly provided for, and say nothing.
choices.outcome: You settle a pension no ledger will explain and a silence no one will thank you for, and you carry Holden's happiness and his grief out of the reach of the station that would only have tidied them away. It is the least official and most human thing you do all year.

choices.label: Do the correct thing — hand it to a charity, close the file.
choices.outcome: You process the matter as the regulations intend: the woman to a mission, the house to the estate, the grave to whatever grows over graves no one is left to tend. Everything is in order. You have done nothing wrong that a court could name, and you cannot for the life of you feel clean.

choices.label: Pay to keep the child's grave, and send her home to her people.
choices.outcome: You cannot mend it, but you keep one small grave from vanishing and send one woman back to her own people with something in her hand and her dignity whole. Years later the grave is still swept, by someone the mali will not name.

title: On the City Wall
body: Lalun's house on the old city wall is the pleasantest in the district and the most dangerous — poets, wits, and the men Government watches all take their tobacco there. Tonight, in the confusion of a festival, you are given quietly to understand that an old rebel the Police have wanted for thirty years could be walked out of the city under cover of the crowd, and that no one need ever know your part in it, or in stopping it.

choices.label: Tighten the cordon and take the old man.
choices.outcome: You spring the trap the festival was meant to spoil, and the old rebel — frail, courteous, forty years a legend — is taken quietly in the crowd. Government is pleased. The city, which had made him a story, sets about making him a martyr, and the Police congratulate themselves in triplicate.

choices.label: Let the festival carry him out, and see nothing.
choices.outcome: You find urgent business on the far side of the city for the crucial hour, and an old man vanishes into the country he loves to die in his own time. You have failed in your plain duty and you sleep, irritatingly, rather well on it.

choices.label: Go yourself to Lalun's and learn who is using whom.
choices.outcome: You spend a strange evening among the poets and the plotters and come away knowing, for once, the true shape of the game — who is loyal, who is bought, who is merely lonely. It is worth more than any arrest, and it can be entered in no return. Strickland would approve. The Commissioner must never know.

title: A Turn at the Great Game
body: A cypher telegram from the Residency: a man will come to you carrying half a torn banknote; you are to match it against the half enclosed, ask him nothing, and pass him north with horses and silence. It is the Great Game — the quiet war of the passes that appears in no budget and no honours list — and you have been handed a small, deniable piece of it.

choices.label: Play your part to the letter, and ask nothing.
choices.outcome: You match the note, mount the stranger, and watch him ride into the dark toward whatever the frontier is buying or selling this season. You will never know his name or his errand or whether either was worth a life; only that a great quiet machine turned once, in your district, on your word, and moved on.

choices.label: Help him, but quietly learn who he is.
choices.outcome: You do as bidden and, being a curious man in a dangerous trade, you also find out a little more than you were meant to. The knowledge is a weight and not a shield. In the Great Game, the men who know most are the men found face-down in the snow of a pass no map admits exists.

choices.label: Wire back that your district is not a corridor for the Residency's spies.
choices.outcome: You decline, on paper, to play, and the cypher traffic goes cold and finds another, more obliging magistrate up the line. You have kept your hands out of a filthy business, and marked yourself, in a quarter that never forgets, as a man who would not be useful. The cypher clerks stop saluting you first.
